# Crank--Nicolson Method

## Biological problem

We consider a substance with concentration $u(x,t)$ that diffuses in one spatial dimension with a constant diffusion coefficient $D$. Point-like agents that act as sources and sinks in this one dimensional space. They may secrete the substance into the environment or remove it through uptake. These point-like agents might represent individual bacterium or discrete protein clusters positioned at specific locations along a filament or channel.

:::{.callout-note title="Dimensions and units"}

We use the following dimensions and units:

- $M$ denotes 'amount of substance' (e.g. units of moles, molecules, or mass).
- $L$ denotes the length (e.g. µm), 
- $T$ denotes time (e.g. seconds).

Where dimension-generic expressions are given, $d$ denotes the number of spatial dimensions. For this document $d=1$.
:::

 

## Equation to solve

The governing diffusion--reaction equation is

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}
=
D \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}
+
O(x)
-
I(x,u,t).
$$ {#eq-diffusion-source-sink}

Here,

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|---|---|---|
| $u(x,t)$ | Extracellular concentration | $M/L^d$ |
| $\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}$ | Second spatial derivative | $M/L^{d+2}$ |
| $D$ | Diffusion coefficient | $L^2/T$ |
| $O(x)$ | Source term (production of $u$) | $M/(L^d\,T)$ |
| $I(x,u,t)$ | Sink term (uptake of $u$) | $M/(L^d\,T)$ |

Let $B_o$ denote the set of secreting agents and $B_i$ the set of consuming agents and let $x_s$ be the position of agent $s$; the agents are then represented as point-like sources and sinks using Dirac delta functions

$$
O(x)
=
K_O
\sum_{s\in B_o}
\delta(x-x_s), 
$$

$$
I(x,u,t)
=
K_I\,u(x,t)
\sum_{s\in B_i}
\delta(x-x_s).
$$

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|---|---|---|
| $K_O$ | Per-agent secretion rate (point-source strength) | $M/T$ |
| $K_I$ | Per-agent first-order uptake coefficient | $L^d/T$ |



## Discretization



```{ojs}
//|code-fold: true
d3 = require("d3@7")

drawGrid = (N) => {
    const width = 420, height = 240;
    const marginX = 60;

    const displayItems = (() => {
      if (N <= 5) {
        return d3.range(N).map(i => ({ type: "node", i, x: i, indexLabel: String(i) }));
      }
      return [
        { type: "node", i: 0, x: 0, indexLabel: "0" },
        { type: "node", i: 1, x: 1, indexLabel: "1" },
        { type: "node", i: 2, x: 2, indexLabel: "2" },
        { type: "dots" },
        { type: "node", i: N - 2, x: N - 2, indexLabel: "N-2" },
        { type: "node", i: N - 1, x: N - 1, indexLabel: "N-1" }
      ];
    })();

  const nodeItems = displayItems.filter(d => d.type === "node");

  const yN  = 90;  // baseline for time level n
  const yN1 = 190; // baseline for time level n+1

  const x = d3.scaleLinear()
      .domain([0, N - 1])
      .range([marginX, width - marginX]);

  const svg = d3.create("svg")
      .attr("width", width)
      .attr("height", height);

  svg.append("defs").append("marker")
      .attr("id", "arrow")
      .attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10")
      .attr("refX", 5).attr("refY", 5)
      .attr("markerWidth", 6).attr("markerHeight", 6)
      .attr("orient", "auto-start-reverse")
    .append("path")
      .attr("d", "M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 Z")
      .attr("fill", "gray");

  function drawRow(y, label) {
    const safeId = label.replace("+", "");

    svg.append("line")
        .attr("x1", x(0)).attr("x2", x(N - 1))
        .attr("y1", y).attr("y2", y)
        .attr("stroke", "black")
        .attr("stroke-width", 1.5);

    svg.selectAll(`circle.row-${safeId}`)
      .data(nodeItems)
      .join("circle")
        .attr("class", `row-${safeId}`)
        .attr("cx", d => x(d.x))
        .attr("cy", y)
        .attr("r", 6)
        .attr("fill", "grey");

    svg.append("text")
        .attr("x", marginX - 25)
        .attr("y", y + 4)
        .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
        .attr("font-weight", "bold")
        .text(label);
  }
  drawRow(yN, "n");
  drawRow(yN1, "n+1");

  displayItems.forEach(d => {
    if (d.type === "node") {
      svg.append("text")
        .attr("x", x(d.x))
        .attr("y", yN - 22)
        .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
        .attr("font-size", "14px")
        .text(d.indexLabel);
    } else {
      svg.append("text")
        .attr("x", (x(2) + x(N - 2)) / 2)
        .attr("y", yN - 22)
        .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
        .attr("font-size", "12px")
        .text("…");
    }
  });

  nodeItems.forEach(d => {
    svg.append("line")
        .attr("x1", x(d.x)).attr("x2", x(d.x))
        .attr("y1", yN + 6).attr("y2", yN1 - 6)
        .attr("stroke", "lightgray")
        .attr("stroke-dasharray", "3,3");
  });

  svg.append("line")
      .attr("x1", marginX - 25).attr("x2", marginX - 25)
      .attr("y1", yN + 15).attr("y2", yN1 - 15)
      .attr("stroke", "gray")
      .attr("marker-end", "url(#arrow)")
      .attr("marker-start", "url(#arrow)");

  svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", marginX - 45)
      .attr("y", (yN + yN1) / 2 + 4)
      .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
      .text("Δt");

  svg.append("line")
      .attr("x1", x(0)+12).attr("x2", x(1)-12)
      .attr("y1", yN - 25).attr("y2", yN - 25)
      .attr("stroke", "gray")
      .attr("marker-end", "url(#arrow)")
      .attr("marker-start", "url(#arrow)");

  svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", (x(0) + x(1)) / 2)
      .attr("y", yN - 32)
      .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
      .text("Δx");

  svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", width / 2)
      .attr("y", 15)   // was 20
      .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
      .attr("font-weight", "bold")
      .text("Crank–Nicolson space–time grid");

  const container = document.createElement("div");
  container.style.textAlign = "center";
  container.appendChild(svg.node());
  return container;
}

schematicN6 = drawGrid(6) // number of grid points, indices 0..5
```

### space and time discretization

The domain is discretized on a uniform grid of `N` ($N$) points with spacing `dx` $\Delta x$ and time step `dt` $\Delta t$. The  array `u`
stores $u_i^n$, which approximates $u(x_i, t^n)$. Of these four parameters, the only one that will be stored as a global will be `N`, since it will  be used in all parts of the module, includding the hot-code inside  the time stepping loop in @lst-define-cn-time-stepping. On the other hand, `dx` and `dt` will only  be used to calculate nondimentional diffusion parameters and reaction terms (see @lst-define-cn-set-parameters)


`N` is declared as

```{.typescript #lst-declare-N lst-cap="lst-declare-N"}
let N: number;
```

together with other global variables in @lst-define-global-variables. `N` is initialized by calling the  function `CNSetSize(N)` with the desired number of grid points (see @lst-define-cn-set-size), which also allocates all arrays that deppend on  grid size.


```{.typescript #lst-assign-N lst-cap="lst-assign-N" }
N = numberOfGridPoints
```










### Laplacian  discretization


The Laplacian is discretized as follows

$$
\nabla^2(u_i^n)
=
\frac{u_{i-1}^n - 2u_i^n + u_{i+1}^n}{\Delta x^2}.
$$ {#eq-laplacian}

### Sinks and sources discretization

Let $m_i^{(O)}$ and $m_i^{(I)}$ denote the number of secreting and consuming agents in grid cell $i$, and let $i_s$ be the grid index of the cell to which agent $s$ is assigned (for example, the nearest grid cell). Then

$$
m_i^{(O)} = \sum_{s\in B_o} \delta_{i,i_s}, \qquad
m_i^{(I)} = \sum_{s\in B_i} \delta_{i,i_s},
$$ {#eq-agents-counts}
Here,  $\delta_{i,i_s}$ is the Kronecker delta, which is dimensionless (unlike the Dirac delta $\delta(x)$ used in the continuous case, which has units of $1/L^d$).

Then, the source and sink terms can be discretized as

$$
O_i
=
\frac{K_O}{\Delta x}
m_i^{(O)}
$$ {#eq-source-discrete}


$$
I_i^n
=
\frac{K_I}{\Delta x}
u_i^n
m_i^{(I)}
$$ {#eq-sink-discrete}

The factor $1/\Delta x$ represents each point-like agent as a source or sink distributed over its assigned grid cell. Consequently, integrating the discrete source or sink over that cell recovers the secretion or uptake associated with that agent. 

The arrays $m^{(I)}$ and $m^{(O)}$ are called `sinks` and `sources` and are passed as arguments to the  function `CNSetParameters()` in @lst-define-cn-set-parameters

```{.typescript #lst-define-cn-set-parameters lst-cap="lst-define-cn-set-parameters"}

export const CNSetParameters = (
    D: number,
    dx: number,
    dt: number,
    K_I: number,
    K_O: number,
    sinks: Float64Array,
    sources: Float64Array,
): void => {

  	
  <<lst-compute-lambda>>
  <<lst-fill-q-beta>>
  <<lst-fill-diagonals>>


};
```





## Crank--Nicolson scheme 

Using the Crank--Nicolson method, the diffusion and uptake terms are averaged between time levels $n$ and $n+1$. Since the secretion term is assumed constant in time, it is included directly:

$$
\frac{u_i^{n+1} - u_i^n}{\Delta t}
=
\frac{D}{2}
\left[
\nabla^2(u_i^{n+1}) + \nabla^2(u_i^n)
\right]
+
O_i
-
\frac{1}{2}
\left[
I_i^{n+1} + I_i^n
\right].
$${#eq-crank-nicolson}

Inserting the explicit forms of the discrete Laplacian, source term and sink term (@eq-laplacian, @eq-source-discrete, @eq-sink-discrete) into
@eq-crank-nicolson and multiplying by $\Delta t$, we arrive at the linear system


$$
\begin{aligned}
u_i^{n+1} - u_i^n
={}&
\frac{D \Delta t}{2 \Delta x^2}
\Bigl[
    u_{i-1}^{n+1}
    - 2u_i^{n+1}
    + u_{i+1}^{n+1}
    + u_{i-1}^{n}
    - 2u_i^{n}
    + u_{i+1}^{n}
\Bigr]
\\
&+
\frac{K_O \Delta t}{\Delta x}
m_i^{(O)}
\\
&-
\frac{K_I \Delta t}{2\Delta x}
m_i^{(I)}
\Bigl[
    u_i^n + u_i^{n+1}
\Bigr]
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-crank-nicolson-expanded}


For convenience, define the parameters $\lambda$ , $q_i$, and $\beta_i$:

$$
\lambda
=
\frac{D \Delta t}{2\Delta x^2}
\qquad
q_i=
\frac{K_O \Delta t}{\Delta x}m_i^{(O)},
\qquad
\beta_i
=
\frac{K_I \Delta t}{2\Delta x}m_i^{(I)}
$$

### Parameter declaration

$\lambda$, $q$, and $\beta$ are declared as

```{.typescript #lst-declare-lambda-q-beta lst-cap="lst-declare-lambda-q-beta"}
let lambda: number;  
let q: Float64Array;
let beta: Float64Array;
```
 in @lst-define-global-variables

### Parameter initialization

The arrays `q` and `beta` are allocated with size `N` by `CNSetSize(N)`:

```{.typescript #lst-alloc-q-beta lst-cap="lst-alloc-q-beta"}
q = new Float64Array(N);
beta = new Float64Array(N);
```

The parameters `lambda`, `q`, and `beta` are then computed by `CNSetParameters()`.

`lambda` is computed as

```{.typescript #lst-compute-lambda lst-cap="lst-compute-lambda"}
lambda = (D * dt) / (2.0 * dx * dx);
```

and the arrays `q` and `beta` are filled using the formulas for $q_i$ and $\beta_i$ derived above:

```{.typescript #lst-fill-q-beta lst-cap="lst-fill-q-beta"}
for (let i: number = 0; i < N; i++) {
	q[i] = (K_O * dt) / dx * sources[i];
	beta[i] = (K_I * dt) / (2.0 * dx) * sinks[i];
}
```

where `D`, `K_O`, and `K_I` are coefficients passed as arguments to `CNSetParameters()`; and `sources` and `sinks` are arrays of length `N` passed as arguments to `CNSetParameters()` containing $m_i^{(O)}$ and $m_i^{(I)}$, respectively.


## Tridiagonal system

Then @eq-crank-nicolson-expanded can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}
u_i^{n+1} - u_i^n
={}&
\lambda
\Bigl[
    u_{i-1}^{n+1}
    - 2u_i^{n+1}
    + u_{i+1}^{n+1}
    + u_{i-1}^{n}
    - 2u_i^{n}
    + u_{i+1}^{n}
\Bigr]
\\
&+
q_i
-
\beta_i
\Bigl[
    u_i^n + u_i^{n+1}
\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
$$

Collecting the unknown terms at time level $n+1$ on the left-hand side gives

$$
- \lambda u_{i-1}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_i\right) u_i^{n+1}
- \lambda u_{i+1}^{n+1}
=
 \lambda u_{i-1}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_i\right) u_i^n
+\lambda u_{i+1}^{n}
+q_i.
$$ {#eq-crank-nicolson-tridiagonal}




This equation applies to every grid point $i=0,\ldots,N-1$, so that for a spatial domain with $N$ grid points, we obtain a system of $N$ linear equations. For a case with Neumann boundary conditions, the system can be written in matrix form as 

$$
A u^{n+1} = d
$$,

where $A$ is the $N \times N$ tridiagonal matrix

$$
A =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 + 2\lambda + \beta_0 & -2\lambda & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
-\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_1 & -\lambda & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & -\lambda & \ddots & \ddots & 0 \\
\vdots & \ddots & \ddots & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_{N-2} & -\lambda \\
0 & \cdots & 0 & -2\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_{N-1}
\end{bmatrix},
$$

$u^{n+1}$ is the unknown vector of concentrations at time level $n+1$,

$$
u^{n+1} =
\begin{bmatrix}
u_0^{n+1} \\
u_1^{n+1} \\
\vdots \\
u_{N-2}^{n+1} \\
u_{N-1}^{n+1}
\end{bmatrix},
$$

and the right-hand side vector $d$ is given by

$$
d =
\begin{bmatrix}
\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_0\right) u_0^n + 2\lambda u_1^n + q_0 \\
\lambda u_0^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_1\right) u_1^n + \lambda u_2^n + q_1 \\
\vdots \\
\lambda u_{N-3}^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_{N-2}\right) u_{N-2}^n + \lambda u_{N-1}^n + q_{N-2} \\
2\lambda u_{N-2}^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_{N-1}\right) u_{N-1}^n + q_{N-1}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Here, the entries of $A$ and $d$ at the boundaries $i=0$ and $i=N-1$ incorporate Neumann (zero-flux) boundary conditions. The solution vector $u^{n+1}$ is solved from the system $A u^{n+1} = d$ using the Thomas algorithm, whose implementation lives in a separate module. 




:::{.callout-note collapse=true title='Example for $N=5$ and Neuman BC'}

```{ojs}
//|code-fold: true
schematicN5 = drawGrid(5)
```

If we apply this equation to $5$ grid points ($i=0,1,2,3,4$), we obtain a system of $5$ linear equations for the unknowns $u_i^{n+1}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}
-{\color{red} \lambda u_{-1}^{n+1}}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_0\right) u_0^{n+1}
- \lambda u_{1}^{n+1}
={}&
{\color{red} \lambda u_{-1}^{n}}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_0\right) u_0^n
+\lambda u_{1}^{n}
+q_0,
\\
- \lambda u_{0}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_1\right) u_1^{n+1}
- \lambda u_{2}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda u_{0}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_1\right) u_1^n
+\lambda u_{2}^{n}
+q_1,
\\
- \lambda u_{1}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_2\right) u_2^{n+1}
- \lambda u_{3}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda u_{1}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_2\right) u_2^n
+\lambda u_{3}^{n}
+q_2,
\\
- \lambda u_{2}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_3\right) u_3^{n+1}
 - \lambda u_{4}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda u_{2}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_3\right) u_3^n
+\lambda u_{4}^{n}
+q_3,
\\
 - \lambda u_{3}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_4\right) u_4^{n+1}
 - {\color{red} \lambda u_{5}^{n+1}}
={}&
 \lambda u_{3}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_4\right) u_4^n
+{\color{red}\lambda u_{5}^{n}}
+q_4.
\end{aligned}
$$
Here, the red terms correspond to cells outside the domain which represent the boundary conditions. These are set to a constant value in the case of Dirichlet boundary conditions, or set via centered difference mirroring in the case of Neumann (zero-flux) boundary conditions. For this implementation, we use Neumann zero-flux boundary conditions. With centered differences, zero flux at the left boundary implies $u_{-1} = u_1$, and at the right boundary $u_{N} = u_{N-2}$. This way, by setting $u_{-1} = u_1$ and $u_5 = u_3$, we can eliminate the red terms, giving 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_0\right) u_0^{n+1} - 2\lambda u_{1}^{n+1}
={}&
\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_0\right) u_0^n
+ 2\lambda u_{1}^{n}
+q_0,
\\
- \lambda u_{0}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_1\right) u_1^{n+1}
- \lambda u_{2}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda u_{0}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_1\right) u_1^n
+\lambda u_{2}^{n}
+q_1,
\\
- \lambda u_{1}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_2\right) u_2^{n+1}
- \lambda u_{3}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda u_{1}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_2\right) u_2^n
+\lambda u_{3}^{n}
+q_2,
\\
- \lambda u_{2}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_3\right) u_3^{n+1}
- \lambda u_{4}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda u_{2}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_3\right) u_3^n
+\lambda u_{4}^{n}
+q_3,
\\
- 2\lambda u_{3}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_4\right) u_4^{n+1}
={}&
 2\lambda u_{3}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_4\right) u_4^n
+q_4.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a tridiagonal system that can be represented in matrix form as $A u^{n+1} = d$, where $A$ is

$$
A =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 + 2\lambda + \beta_0 & -2\lambda & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
-\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_1 & -\lambda & 0 & 0 \\
0 & -\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_2 & -\lambda & 0 \\
0 & 0 & -\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_3 & -\lambda \\
0 & 0 & 0 & -2\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_4
\end{bmatrix},
$$

$u^{n+1}$ is

$$
u^{n+1} =
\begin{bmatrix}
u_0^{n+1} \\
u_1^{n+1} \\
u_2^{n+1} \\
u_3^{n+1} \\
u_4^{n+1}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

and the right-hand side vector $d$ is
$$
d =
\begin{bmatrix}
\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_0\right) u_0^n + 2\lambda u_1^n + q_0 \\
\lambda u_0^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_1\right) u_1^n + \lambda u_2^n + q_1 \\
\lambda u_1^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_2\right) u_2^n + \lambda u_3^n + q_2 \\
\lambda u_2^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_3\right) u_3^n + \lambda u_4^n + q_3 \\
2\lambda u_3^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_4\right) u_4^n + q_4
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

:::

## Building the tridiagonal matrix $A$


The matrix $A$ is built from the lower, main, and upper diagonals.

### Diagonals declaration
 
The three diagonals are declared in @lst-define-global-variables as


```{.typescript #lst-declare-diagonals lst-cap="lst-declare-diagonals"}
let lowerDiagonal: Float64Array;
let mainDiagonal: Float64Array;
let upperDiagonal: Float64Array;
```

### Diagonals initialization

The diagonals are allocated with size `N` by `CNSetSize(N)`:

```{.typescript #lst-alloc-diagonals lst-cap="lst-alloc-diagonals"}
lowerDiagonal = new Float64Array(N);
mainDiagonal = new Float64Array(N);
upperDiagonal = new Float64Array(N);
```

and then filled with their corresponding parameter values by `CNSetParameters()`:

```{.typescript #lst-fill-diagonals lst-cap="lst-fill-diagonals"}
for (let i: number = 1; i < N - 1; i++) {
  lowerDiagonal[i] = -lambda;
  mainDiagonal[i] = 1.0 + 2.0 * lambda + beta[i];
  upperDiagonal[i] = -lambda;
}

lowerDiagonal[0] = 0.0;
mainDiagonal[0] = 1.0 + 2.0 * lambda + beta[0];
upperDiagonal[0] = -2.0 * lambda;

lowerDiagonal[N - 1] = -2.0 * lambda;
mainDiagonal[N - 1] = 1.0 + 2.0 * lambda + beta[N - 1];
upperDiagonal[N - 1] = 0.0;

```


## Building the right hand side

The entries of the right-hand side vector $d$ is given by @eq-crank-nicolson-tridiagonal. For interior grid points $i = 1,\ldots,N-2$, each entry is

$$
d_i = \lambda u_{i-1}^n + (1 - 2\lambda - \beta_i) u_i^n + \lambda u_{i+1}^n + q_i.
$$

To handle the Neumann (zero-flux) boundary conditions we use centered differences to mirror the ghost cells. At the left boundary ($i=0$), zero flux implies $u_{-1} = u_1$, giving

$$
\begin{aligned}
d_0
&= \lambda u_{-1}^n + (1 - 2\lambda - \beta_0) u_0^n + \lambda u_1^n + q_0 \\
&= (1 - 2\lambda - \beta_0) u_0^n + 2\lambda u_1^n + q_0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, at the right boundary ($i=N-1$), $u_N = u_{N-2}$, so

$$
d_{N-1} = (1 - 2\lambda - \beta_{N-1}) u_{N-1}^n+  2\lambda u_{N-2}^n + q_{N-1}.
$$

The ghost-cell mirroring is implemented directly in the code that builds $d$ at each time step inside @lst-define-cn-time-stepping

```{.typescript #lst-compute-rhs-vector lst-cap="lst-compute-rhs-vector"}

for (let i: number = 1; i < N - 1; i++) {
	d[i] = lambda * u[i - 1] 
		+ (1.0 - 2.0 * lambda - beta[i]) * u[i]  
		+ lambda * u[i + 1] 
		+ q[i];
}

d[0] = (1.0 - 2.0 * lambda - beta[0]) * u[0] 
	+ 2.0 * lambda * u[1] 
	+ q[0];

d[N - 1] = (1.0 - 2.0 * lambda - beta[N - 1]) * u[N - 1] 
	+ 2.0 * lambda * u[N - 2]  
	+ q[N - 1];
```


## Module structure

The typescript file that implements this numerical method is organized into four main sections: @lst-define-global-variables, @lst-define-cn-set-size, @lst-define-cn-set-parameters, and @lst-define-cn-time-stepping.


```{.typescript file=src/crankNicolson.ts filename="src/crankNicolson.ts"}

<<lst-define-global-variables>>

<<lst-define-cn-set-size>>

<<lst-define-cn-set-parameters>>

<<lst-define-cn-time-stepping>>

```

In @lst-define-global-variables we define the arrays and variables that are shared across the whole module. In @lst-define-cn-set-size we allocate all arrays that deppend on grid size. In @lst-define-cn-set-parameters we precompute coefficients and fill the diagonals.

```{.typescript #lst-define-cn-set-size lst-cap="lst-define-cn-set-size"}

export const CNSetSize = (
    numberOfGridPoints: number,
): void => {

  <<lst-assign-N>>
  <<lst-alloc-q-beta>>
  <<lst-alloc-diagonals>>
  <<lst-alloc-thomas-scratch-arrays>>

};
```


And in @lst-define-cn-time-stepping we will implement the time-stepping loop that advances the solution by solving the tridiagonal system at each step.

```{.typescript #lst-define-cn-time-stepping lst-cap="lst-define-cn-time-stepping"}

export const CNTimeStepping = (
    u: Float64Array,
    totalNumberOfIterations: number,
): void => {


	<<lst-define-time-stepping-logic>>


};
```







## Thomas‑solver scratch arrays

The Thomas algorithm modifies the right‑hand side in place during forward elimination and needs a scratch buffer for the modified upper diagonal. Pre‑allocating these at module scope avoids re‑allocating on every time step.


### Scratch arrays declaration

They are declared at @lst-define-global-variables as

```{.typescript #lst-declare-thomas-scratch-arrays lst-cap="lst-declare-thomas-scratch-arrays"}
let modifiedUpper: Float64Array;
let d: Float64Array;
```

### Scratch arrays allocation

They are allocated by `CNSetSize(N)` as

```{.typescript #lst-alloc-thomas-scratch-arrays lst-cap="lst-alloc-thomas-scratch-arrays"}
modifiedUpper = new Float64Array(N);
d = new Float64Array(N);
```


## Module‑level state

We collect all the module‑level variables in the first part of the module together with the import of the Thomas algorithm


```{.typescript #lst-define-global-variables lst-cap="lst-define-global-variables"}
import { thomasAlgorithm } from "./thomasAlgorithm.js";
<<lst-declare-N>>
<<lst-declare-lambda-q-beta>>
<<lst-declare-diagonals>>
<<lst-declare-thomas-scratch-arrays>>
```




## The time‑stepping loop

We first need to copy the array of concentrations given by the caller into `u`, then iterate for the requested number of steps. And finally, write the result back into the provided `concentration` array.


```{.typescript #lst-define-time-stepping-logic lst-cap="lst-define-time-stepping-logic"}
    


for (let step: number = 0; step < totalNumberOfIterations; step++) {

  <<lst-compute-rhs-vector>>

  thomasAlgorithm(
    lowerDiagonal,
    mainDiagonal,
    upperDiagonal,
    d,
    N,
    modifiedUpper,
    u,
  );

}




```
